hood_landmark.Ala Moana: Ala Moana Center, the world's largest open-air shopping mall

avoid.reason: Very safe; car break-ins and theft at beaches/trailheads — leave nothing in cars

hood_desc: Waikiki is the iconic high-rise beach resort district packed with hotels, shopping and nightlife, best for first-time visitors and beach lovers who want to be in the middle of the action.
Ala Moana centers on a massive open-air mall and a calm beach park, suiting shoppers and travelers who want a central base near Waikiki without the resort crowds.
Chinatown is a historic downtown quarter with lively markets, art galleries, lei shops and buzzing restaurants, great for foodies and culture seekers though grittier after dark.

Honolulu's most affluent seaside neighbourhood, east of Diamond Head: quiet tree-lined avenues, the sheltered Waialae and Kahala beaches, and Kahala Mall for shopping and cinema. A calm, residential base about 20 minutes' drive from Waikiki, best suited to travellers with a car who want beach and quiet over nightlife.
lodging: The Royal Hawaiian a Luxury Collection Resort
Aston at the Executive Centre Hotel

water.note: Tap water is treated and safe to drink.

transit.pay: The HOLO card is the main fare card (a $2 one-time fee, then loaded with value or a pass) and is sold at ABC Stores, Foodland, Longs Drugs, vending machines and the HOLO app; conventional contactless bank-card tap is not yet standard, so cash (exact fare) or a HOLO card is best. A single ride is $3.25 and a 24-hour day pass $7.50, valid on both TheBus and Skyline.
transit.hours: Most TheBus routes run from about 4:30am to around midnight (a few late-night routes), while Skyline rail runs daily 4am-10:30pm with no overnight service.
transit.note: TheBus and the expanding Skyline rail cover Honolulu well, but many attractions (North Shore, Hanauma Bay, hiking trails) are far from any route, so most visitors rent a car or use rideshare for full-island exploration.

food.name: Poke
food.desc: Cubed raw ahi tossed with shoyu, sesame oil, sweet onion and limu. Buy it by the pound at a fish counter, not in a build-your-own bowl.

places.name: Ono Seafood
places.note: Family-run for 25-plus years; the shoyu ahi with never-frozen fish is the local benchmark.

places.name: Maguro Brothers Hawaii
places.note: Former Tsukiji fishmongers buying daily at the Honolulu fish auction; try the hamachi bowl.

places.name: Fresh Catch
places.note: Local fish market and plate lunch counter with a long list of poke styles by the pound.

food.name: Plate lunch
food.desc: Hawaii's working lunch: two scoops rice, one scoop macaroni salad and a protein such as kalbi, shoyu chicken or chicken katsu, in a foam clamshell.

places.name: Rainbow Drive-In
places.note: Feeding Honolulu since 1961 and still the plate lunch locals name first.

places.name: Highway Inn
places.note: Third-generation family restaurant pairing plate lunch with traditional Hawaiian sides.

places.name: Kahai Street Kitchen
places.note: Chef-run lunch counter with a rotating menu; office workers queue before noon.

food.name: Loco moco
food.desc: White rice, a hamburger patty, brown gravy and a fried egg over the top. Invented on the Big Island in 1949 and now a statewide comfort food.

places.name: Rainbow Drive-In
places.note: The classic version with its own chili-style gravy; eat it at the outdoor tables.

places.name: Liliha Bakery
places.note: Open long hours at the counter; follow it with a Coco Puff cream puff.

places.name: Zippy's
places.note: Island-wide diner chain and the reliable 2am loco moco option.

food.name: Malasada
food.desc: Portuguese yeast doughnut with no hole, fried to order and rolled in sugar, sometimes filled with haupia coconut or custard. Best eaten hot in the parking lot.

places.name: Leonard's Bakery
places.note: Making them since 1952; the pink neon sign is a Honolulu landmark. Get them hot.

places.name: Kamehameha Bakery
places.note: Locals' early-morning pick, famous for the purple poi glazed malasada.

places.name: Pipeline Bakeshop and Creamery
places.note: Small neighborhood shop known for lighter malasadas and good ice cream.

food.name: Shave ice
food.desc: Ice shaved to snow, soaked in tropical syrups, often over ice cream and azuki beans with a snow cap of condensed milk. Not a snow cone.

places.name: Waiola Shave Ice
places.note: Famously fine, pillowy ice and five boards of flavors; the in-town standard.

places.name: Uncle Clay's House of Pure Aloha
places.note: Syrups made from real fruit rather than concentrate, and genuinely warm service.

places.name: Shimazu Store
places.note: Enormous portions at neighborhood prices; a longtime local favorite.

food.name: Hawaiian kalua pig and laulau
food.desc: Salt-cured pork smoked underground in an imu, plus pork and butterfish steamed in taro leaves, served with poi, lomi salmon and haupia.

places.name: Helena's Hawaiian Food
places.note: James Beard America's Classic since 1946; the pipikaula short ribs are essential.

places.name: Young's Fish Market
places.note: Takeout counter widely rated for the best laulau on Oahu.

places.name: Haili's Hawaiian Foods
places.note: Family-run since 1950, serving traditional plates and fresh poi.

food.name: POG
food.desc: Passion fruit, orange and guava juice, created on Maui in 1971 and now the default island soft drink, sold cold in every store and cafe.

places.name: ABC Stores
places.note: On practically every Waikiki corner; grab a cold carton on the way to the beach.

places.name: Rainbow Drive-In
places.note: The classic pairing: a POG alongside a loco moco plate.

places.name: Foodland
places.note: Local supermarket chain stocking Hawaiian Sun POG and other island juices.

food.name: Mai tai
food.desc: Rum, lime, orgeat and orange curacao. The Waikiki version usually adds passion-orange-guava juice and a float of dark rum, served at sunset.

places.name: Mai Tai Bar at The Royal Hawaiian
places.note: Beachfront at the pink hotel where the drink was popularized in Hawaii in 1953.

places.name: House Without a Key
places.note: Sunset hula and live Hawaiian music under a century-old kiawe tree.

places.name: Duke's Waikiki
places.note: Loud, cheerful and right on the sand; the everyday tourist classic done well.

landmarks: Diamond Head
An iconic volcanic tuff cone crater looming over Waikiki, offering one of Oahu's most recognizable skyline silhouettes and summit views.
Waikīkī Beach
Hawaii's most famous stretch of sand, with turquoise water, surfers, and Diamond Head as a dramatic backdrop.
USS Arizona Memorial
A solemn floating memorial spanning the sunken battleship at Pearl Harbor, a deeply moving and historic photo subject.
ʻIolani Palace
The only official state residence of royalty on US soil, a beautifully restored 19th-century palace in downtown Honolulu.
Hanauma Bay
A stunning volcanic crater bay with clear turquoise waters and coral reefs, one of Oahu's most scenic snorkeling spots.
Byōdō-In Temple
A serene replica of a 900-year-old Japanese temple nestled against the lush Koʻolau mountains, with reflecting ponds and peacocks.
Kawaiahaʻo Church
A historic 19th-century coral-block church known as Hawaii's 'Westminster Abbey,' tied to the Hawaiian monarchy.
USS Missouri Memorial
The 'Mighty Mo' battleship where Japan formally surrendered in WWII, now a massive floating museum moored at Pearl Harbor.
Ala Moana Beach Park
A popular calm-water urban beach park with a scenic lagoon and skyline views, a favorite for sunset photography.
Bishop Museum
Hawaii's largest museum, founded in 1889 in the Kalihi district to house Princess Bernice Pauahi Bishop's royal Hawaiian artifacts, now the leading repository of Pacific natural and cultural history.

train.note: Hawaii has no intercity or international trains. Honolulu's only rail is Skyline (https://honolulutransit.org/), an urban metro across southern Oahu that is still being extended toward downtown - it is local transit, not travel between islands. Nothing on the network connects to another city or another island, so treat air travel as the equivalent of intercity rail here.

bus.note: There are no intercity or international buses - Honolulu is on an island in the middle of the Pacific. TheBus (https://www.thebus.org/) covers the whole island of Oahu cheaply and reliably, including the airport, Waikiki and the North Shore, and is the practical way to get around without a car; travel to the other Hawaiian islands is by air. Fares are paid by tap card or cash on board.

ferry.note: There are no passenger ferries from Honolulu - the Hawaii Superferry between the islands shut down in 2009 and has not been replaced, so inter-island travel is by plane. Only local harbour cruises, whale-watching trips and dinner sails operate from Honolulu Harbor and Kewalo Basin.

half.name: North Shore (Haleiwa)
half.blurb: Laid-back surf coast with giant winter waves, food trucks, and sea turtles.

half.name: Kailua & Lanikai Beach
half.blurb: Powdery white sands and turquoise water rank among the world's finest beaches.

half.name: Kualoa Ranch
half.blurb: Dramatic emerald valley and famous film location beneath towering jungle-clad cliffs.

half.name: Nuuanu Pali Lookout
half.blurb: Windswept clifftop lookout with sweeping views over Oahu's lush eastern coast.

half.name: Waimea Valley
half.blurb: Lush botanical valley with a garden trail leading to a swimmable waterfall.
